title: The three gunas
hookLine: Arjuna once asked what pushes us to do wrong; chapter fourteen names the three threads woven through everything
carry: nature is woven of three gunas
last: THE SAME LORD IN EVERY BEING.

lines: WHAT PUSHES US TO DO WRONG?
cards: Back in chapter three, Arjuna asked Krishna a question almost everyone has asked. What pushes a person to do wrong, even when they don't want to, as if by force?
Krishna's answer was short: it's desire, it's anger, born of rajas. Arjuna didn't get the whole map then. Eleven chapters later, he does.
Chapter fourteen names the three forces Hindu thought sees in everything in nature: in food, in music, in mornings and moods, and in Arjuna too.

teach.b: Sattva, rajas, tamas: these gunas, born of nature, bind the undying one in the body. Guna means a quality, and in ordinary Sanskrit it can also mean a strand or a thread, even the cord of a bowstring.
So picture a rope of three strands twisted together. Everything in nature is all three, in different mixes. Sattva is clarity, brightness, balance.
Verse six: it's clear, it lights things up, it's free of trouble. But even sattva binds, by attachment to happiness and to knowledge. You can get hooked on feeling good and feeling wise.
Rajas is passion, motion, heat. Verse seven: it comes from craving and attachment, and binds by attachment to action. It's the part of you that can't stop doing.
Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia. Verse eight: born of ignorance, it deludes, and binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep.

Verse nine sums up: sattva ties you to happiness, rajas to action, and tamas covers understanding and ties you to heedlessness. So none of the three is simply the good one. Even the bright thread is still a thread.
And some teachers stress that this is a description, not a verdict: rest needs a little tamas, and getting out of bed needs a little rajas. The point isn't to hate any strand. It's to see the rope.
Our word is the first and clearest of the three: sattva.

how: The three gunas are part of Hindu vocabulary: some people describe foods, habits, music and moods as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, and Ayurveda and yoga teachers use the terms too.

o: a calm stillness reached only in long meditation
clarity and brightness, one of nature's three threads
a single strand that, unlike the others, can never bind you

games.q: the three threads — tap the pairs.
p: clarity: binds by happiness and knowledge
a quality; also a strand, a thread

s: in Gita 14, sattva is the one strand that never binds
verse 6: even sattva binds, by attachment to happiness and knowledge.
guna can mean a strand or thread as well as a quality
picture a rope of three strands twisted together.
the Gita names onion and garlic as tamasic
Gita 17 sorts food by the gunas but names neither; leaving them out comes from other texts and family custom.

games.q: you've found sattva: clear, bright, peaceful. according to the Gita, are you free now?
o: not yet: sattva binds too, through attachment to happiness and knowledge.
no: sattva is the worst of the three.
games.why: not yet. verse 6 says even the bright thread binds. chapter 14 will end by pointing beyond all three.

practice: Check your own rope right now: heaviness or a pull toward blankness is the dark thread; buzzing, a list running, is the moving thread; any clarity, even a moment of simply seeing, is the bright one.

Don't pick a favorite; just notice the mix. At your next meal, look at the plate the way Gita seventeen sorts food: fresh and nourishing is sattva; very sharp, salty or burning is rajas; stale and leftover is tamas.

wordCard.voice: Sattva. Clarity, brightness, balance: the first of the three gunas, the strands of nature, with rajas, motion, and tamas, heaviness.

orig.note: Sanskrit: guna, quality; also a strand, a thread, a bowstring. sattva, rajas and tamas are the three gunas.

carryVoice: Your line: nature is woven of three gunas. Clarity, motion, heaviness, twisted into one rope. That's day two hundred seven.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.1–14.4 (the chapter's opening: the highest knowledge; nature as the womb)
Bhagavad Gita 3.36–3.37 (Arjuna: what drives us to wrong? Desire and anger, born of rajas)
Bhagavad Gita 17.8–17.10 (food dear to each guna)
